newsitem.title: USA: Officials say Albright weighs Middle East trip.
newsitem.headline: Officials say Albright weighs Middle East trip.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was on Thursday seriously considering a visit to the Middle East in the wake of a suicide bombing that killed 15 people in Jerusalem, U.S. officials said.
A senior State Department official said, "There is serious consideration being given for the secretary of state to make a trip to the Middle East soon."
But the official, who asked not to be identified, ruled out the possibility of Albright travelling as early as next week, saying Israel needed time to mourn its victims.

"Right now, with Israel in a period of mourning, with the focus of attention on resuming the security cooperation at a strong level, this is not the most opportune moment for her to go. But she certainly will go in the future," National Security Adviser Sandy Berger told CNN.

The State Department official said "a number of options" were under consideration for helping to resume the peace process, adding that it was essential for Palestinian leaders to restore full security cooperation with Israel.

The disclosure that a trip was under consideration came after Albright, just back from an Asian tour, and other top U.S. officials met at the White House to discuss how to advance the peace process after Wednesday's bombing.
U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross had been due to visit the region from Thursday, but postponed his trip indefinitely after the bombing to allow a mourning period in Israel.
Albright has not visited the Middle East since she took office in January, but has vigorously denied suggestions that she is neglecting the region.

Apart from Albright, the hour-long White House meeting also included Ross, Berger, National Security Council desk officer Bruce Riedel and Leon Fuerth, Vice President Al Gore's foreign policy adviser.
"They discussed the situation in the wake of the bombing. No decisions were made. It was not a decision-making meeting. More discussions will follow," White House spokeswoman Anne Luzzatto said.
Berger, speaking to CNN after the meeting, expressed confidence that the bombing would not kill the peace process.
"It's obviously a setback but it cannot be permitted to be fatal ... to the peace process," Berger said. "It will resume. There are some first things that have to be done."

Wednesday's attack at a Jerusalem market was the deadliest since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu won election in 1996 vowing to bolster security. The Islamic militant movement Hamas claimed responsibility.

Clinton on Wednesday condemned the latest violent deed in the Middle East as a barbarous act, and called on Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to take concrete steps to strengthen security in the region.

"Arafat has made some efforts in security cooperation. They have been uneven," Berger said. "We have said this to him in the last 24 hours. There needs to be an intensification of the effort of the Palestinian Authority to crack down on these kinds of terrorist individuals."
"There's no 100 percent results ... but there has to be a 100 percent effort, and we believe there needs to be a greater effort," he said.
The law that makes it possible for Washington to give aid to the Palestinian Authority expires on Aug. 12, and the White House faces major congressional opposition to extending it.

State Department officials said, however, the lapse of the law would not affect the bulk of U.S. aid to the Palestinians, which does not go through the Authority. They said the PLO office in Washington would have to "suspend operations" for the time being but U.S. contacts with the PLO could continue.

Asked if the president was satisfied with Arafat's pledge that he is committed to ensuring a secure environment for Israel, White House spokesman Mike McCurry replied: "The president feels the chairman made an appropriate statement, yes, but ... continues to believe that efforts need to be made to strengthen security cooperation."
